root_idea.summary: The root centers on pressing, squeezing, or compressing something, whether physically, in articulation, or figuratively through forceful prompting and censure.
root_idea.development: Its semantic range develops from physical pressure to pushing and goading, compressed pronunciation, the devil's pressing suggestions, and verbal fault-finding or defamation.

qac_form_accounting.reason: The Quranic plural is presented under the supported singular lexical citation هَمْزَة.

senses.definition: An evil prompting or suggestion of the devils.
senses.usage_conditions: Used in the Quranic construction هَمَزَاتِ الشَّيَاطِينِ for what devils inspire into the human mind.

senses.definition: A defamer or slanderer, one who speaks ill of others.
senses.usage_conditions: A person-designating form whose usage includes fault-finding, backbiting, and repeated or intensive disparagement.

senses.definition: A fault-finder, backbiter, or defamer who speaks ill of others.
senses.usage_conditions: Applied to a man or woman; the described conduct may include reproach behind the back, verbal defamation, or disparaging signs and gestures.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To press, squeeze, or pinch something; also to compress a head or straighten a spear-shaft by such pressure.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A physical transitive use, with the object understood broadly.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To push, impel, or repel a person or thing; to drive someone toward another person or thing.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Includes the conventional expression for a need driving or impelling someone toward someone or something.
A physical action distinct from pressing or impelling.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To goad or spur, urging an animal onward.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Used of urging an animal to move or run, especially with a goad or spur.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To blame, reproach, or find fault with someone; to speak ill of or backbite them.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The backbiting use involves mentioning a person's faults or vices behind the person's back, even when the allegations may be true.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To pronounce a letter or word with hamz, the sound represented by ء.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The articulation is described as a compressed or forced emission from the point of utterance.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To be pressed, squeezed, or pinched, or to be pushed; of a word, to be pronounced with hamz.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A Form VII quasi-passive use corresponding to the physical and pronunciation senses of هَمَزَ.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Madness or insanity attributed to the devil's goading, pressing, or pinching.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A figurative interpretation of the devil's hamz, distinct from the Quranic sense of the devil's suggestions.

other_classical_meanings.definition: The hamzah, the letter ء, regarded as a member of the alphabet and a sister of alif.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: هَمْزٌ is the general noun and هَمْزَة the unitary noun for the letter.

other_classical_meanings.definition: One who blames, reproaches, finds fault with, backbites, or defames others.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A person-designating active participle in the same lexical branch as هُمَزَة and هَمَّاز.

other_classical_meanings.definition: An instrument for beating or goading, such as a spur, staff, or stick, sometimes fitted with an iron point, used to urge animals onward.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Its plural may also designate instruments used to pinch and straighten spear-shafts.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A spur: an iron point attached to the boot of one who breaks or trains draught animals.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The attested plurals include forms used for spurs or related goading instruments.

cautions: The Quranic plural هَمَزَات is normalized here under the supported singular citation هَمْزَة, which is distinct in vocalization from هُمَزَة, the defamer.

هَمَّاز and هُمَزَة have overlapping Quranic descriptions; the evidence does not establish a reliable semantic contrast between them. Lane also reports differing analyses of the intensiveness of هُمَزَة and treats its ending as applicable to either sex.
